To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

MOFs are a class of materials in which the chemical and physical properties can be controlled by the design and synthesis of the framework, and that MOFs are an ideal platform for the study of chemical reactions in the solid state.

the chemical environment within the pores of a MOF is controlled by the geometry and connectivity of the metal ions, the ligands, and their arrangement, which is a function of their chemical structure.

the geometric and connectivity aspects of Werner complexes, which have been studied for 120 years, have been extended into the solid state, in a manner that allows for the direct addressability of the molecular units and the ability to have the substrate sample the chemical environments within the framework.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of new MOFs that have the potential to bring about chemical transformations in the pores.
the design and synthesis of MOFs with specific properties, and with the use of those properties to bring about chemical transformations.
the design of metal–organic framework materials that have the capacity to control the chemistry of a substrate in a spatially defined way.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MOFs are the ultimate realization of the concept of coordination complex chemistry.
Werner’s work has provided the basis for the development of MOF chemistry, which in turn is a direct consequence of his work on coordination chemistry.
MOFs provide the opportunity for the design, synthesis, and study of a vast array of new materials, with properties and functions not available in the molecular realm.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the chemistry of MOFs is now a new and important area in chemistry.

the Werner concept of the coordination sphere has been taken from molecular complexes to crystalline MOFs and that this has led to the ability to control the chemistry of the substrate in ways not available to molecular chemistry.

we have been able to use MOF chemistry to develop new chemical environments and chemical transformations that would not be possible otherwise, and to develop new chemical transformations in MOFs that are not possible in molecular complexes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the chemical reactivity of a substrate in an MOF can be controlled by its spatial location within the MOF and the chemical functionality of the MOF at that location.
the ability to control the spatial arrangement and geometry of the molecular units in a MOF can be exploited to control chemical reactivity.

the ability to have multiple chemical environments in MOFs is an important feature that can be exploited to achieve new chemical transformations and that this is not possible with molecular coordination complexes.
